title: Just because a game is on disc doesn’t mean it will work in the future
gist: DoesItPlay's testing of thousands of physical game releases finds 27 percent require downloads to function properly—rising to 34 percent on PS5 and 50 percent on Xbox Series X—meaning that when platform patch servers eventually shut down, a large share of purchased discs become unplayable. Sony's decision to stop producing physical PlayStation games sharpens the stakes.

insights.claim: Across thousands of physical releases tested by DoesItPlay, a full 27 percent require some sort of download to fix game-breaking bugs or obtain core content not stored on the physical media itself.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: A quarter of physical inventory is effectively a license with a hardware token—reframes what consumers actually own in the games market.
insights.locator: Thus far, a full 27 percent of the physical releases

insights.claim: The download-dependency ratio rises to 34 percent for tested PS5 games and 50 percent for Xbox Series X games.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Platform-level divergence of 34 versus 50 percent is a measurable difference in publisher discipline, and a differentiator collectors and preservationists will price in.
insights.locator: That ratio balloons to 34 percent for tested PS5 games

insights.claim: DoesItPlay owner Clemens Itsel says larger companies increasingly treat physical releases with ignorance, and argues there is no reason physical games would die unless a platform holder like Sony deliberately kills them.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Frames the decline of physical media as a supply-side platform decision, not organic demand collapse—relevant to how retail and boutique publishers position.
insights.quote: There is no reason physical games would ever die unless someone like Sony deliberately kills them.
insights.locator: There is a clear trend that physical releases

insights.claim: Sony's recent decision to stop producing physical PlayStation games in the near future is the trigger for renewed attention to whether existing discs actually work standalone.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: The largest console platform exiting physical distribution accelerates the industry's shift to pure licensing—structurally favorable to digital storefront margins.
insights.locator: Sony’s recent decision to stop producing physical PlayStation games

insights.claim: The first failure mode is games shipped on disc in incomplete, bug-filled states requiring patches, with the initial console release of Cyberpunk 2077 the prototypical example of a disc that will one day be virtually unplayable.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Ship-then-patch development practice creates a permanent preservation liability that the industry has not priced.
insights.locator: Often, the games that fail these tests

insights.claim: Failures can be subtle rather than obvious—in Atomfall's physical release, returning to the main hub village made everyone hostile, breaking numerous side quests and making a peaceful playthrough near-impossible.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Subtle breakage means simple 'does it boot' testing understates the problem—the real defect rate is likely higher than headline figures.
insights.locator: For some games, though, the game-breaking failures

insights.claim: The second failure mode is stub discs: recent releases including Doom: The Dark Ages, Indiana Jones and the Great Circle, and The Outer Worlds 2 ship discs containing only a small portion of the full downloadable game.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
entities: Indiana Jones and the Great Circle
insights.so_what: When the disc is a token rather than the product, physical retail loses its remaining functional justification—accelerating shelf-space exit.
insights.locator: Bugs aside, DoesItPlay also documents numerous physical releases

insights.claim: The third failure mode is mandatory early download prompts that halt all progress without an Internet connection, used by Hogwarts Legacy, Jedi Survivor, The Elder Scrolls IV Oblivion Remaster, 007 First Light, Crimson Desert, Gothic Remake, and almost every modern AAA Ubisoft game.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Deliberate online gating even on complete discs shows publishers actively choosing telemetry and account linkage over offline functionality.
insights.locator: Itsel said he has also noticed a new “blood boiling” trend

insights.claim: Itsel names Microsoft the worst offender, saying Xbox has long given up on producing fully functioning physical releases, too often requiring downloads or forcing players to create a Microsoft account.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Account-mandatory physical media is a deliberate identity-capture strategy—consistent with Microsoft's broader Game Pass and services pivot.
insights.quote: It’s deliberately undermining the value of physical releases by making them incomplete or online-dependent in other ways.
insights.locator: Looking across the major console platform makers

insights.claim: Sony's physical releases are more playable as is, but Itsel observes a decline over recent years in the number of PlayStation discs requiring no downloads.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Directional deterioration at the better-performing platform suggests the trend is industry-wide rather than vendor-specific.
insights.locator: While Sony’s physical releases tend to be more playable

insights.claim: Switch and Switch 2 cartridges often fare better offline, but more publishers are opting for Game Key Cards containing no offline data, which Itsel considers a form of deception.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Selling a download key in physical packaging invites consumer-protection scrutiny—a latent regulatory risk for publishers.
insights.locator: Physical game cartridges on the Switch and Switch 2

insights.claim: Patch dependency is a minor annoyance today, but when centralized platform servers holding those patches eventually shut down, countless game discs become essentially unplayable coasters.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: A dated, deterministic obsolescence mechanism for a large installed base—the clearest argument that 'ownership' of digital-era games is temporary.

insights.claim: Even where Nintendo promises in FAQs that previous purchases and updates on older platforms remain downloadable 'for the foreseeable future', Itsel says server shutdown is just an eventuality.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Corporate 'foreseeable future' commitments carry no enforceable duration—treat them as expiring by default.
insights.locator: Even as companies like Nintendo promise in FAQs

insights.claim: Itsel argues current server stability is irrelevant because upkeep is decided purely by financials and licensing agreements, and consumers allowed purchases to be relabeled as licensing.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: The purchase-to-license relabeling is the structural shift that transferred durable value from consumers to platform holders—visible across software, media, and increasingly hardware.
insights.quote: They can do whatever they want with your games, because we let them relabel a purchase into ‘licensing.’

insights.claim: The 2021 'CBOMB' kill-switch, which threatened to make offline PS3 and PS4 consoles practically useless once internal CMOS clock batteries failed, was eventually fixed on PS4 but the PS3 remains unpatched.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: A precedent where community pressure forced a fix on the current-gen platform but not the legacy one—shows the practical limit of preservation advocacy.
insights.locator: In 2021, the group helped bring wider attention

insights.claim: Itsel sees a rise in boutique labels and smaller publishers serving the passionate physical-media audience, driven on the supply side by developers wanting their work immortalized and an additional revenue stream on top of digital distribution.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: A viable niche physical market persists even as majors exit—an addressable segment for specialist publishers with better unit economics than mass retail.
insights.locator: While companies like Sony are showing an increasing disregard

insights.claim: DoesItPlay began in 2019 as a passion-project Twitter account by Jon Doyle, who went on to found boutique physical publisher Lost in Cult, and has grown into a publicly searchable database of thousands of tested titles.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Community testing infrastructure now produces the only systematic data on physical-release completeness—a dataset with real diligence value.

insights.claim: Itsel acknowledges consumer indifference is the main obstacle, meeting dismissive arguments like 'nobody cares' and 'every game needs a download anyway' from people unaware of the independence and longevity advantages of physical media.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Weak consumer demand for preservation means the market will not self-correct—change requires regulation or the boutique niche, not mass behavior.
insights.quote: If they cared about how these companies treated the art and the customers there would be daily riots in front of every AAA gaming HQ across the planet,
insights.locator: Getting today’s players to care about this problem
